preamble: Raising of the first element of the diphthong [au] to [o] under the influence of the following rounded glide gives [ou] (in effect assimilation of the nucleus to its offglide). Latin au became ou in Galician-Portuguese (aurum > ouro), and Proto-Germanic *au became ou in Old High German except before r, h and dentals, where it went further to ō. The English Great Vowel Shift does not belong here: Middle English stone had [ɔː], not [au], and its path [ɔː] > [oː] > [oʊ] is a monophthong change (see o_to_ou).

examples.note: Old Galician-Portuguese ouro; northern European Portuguese keeps [ˈowɾu], southern European Portuguese has gone on to monophthongal [o], and elsewhere the glide is optional.
Compare Spanish poco, where au went straight to o.
The variant toiro shows the later ou ~ oi alternation.
Compare Gothic augō and Old Norse auga, which keep au.
Except before r, h and dentals, au stayed a diphthong and was raised to ou (here before a labial).
Contrast *dauþu > tōd 'death', where au before a dental monophthongized to ō instead.

sources: Alkire, T., & Rosen, C. (2010). Romance Languages: A Historical Introduction. Cambridge University Press.
